title: NINE STATES

suspect.name: Daniel Shays
suspect.portrait_alt: A 1787 woodcut of two men in coats and hats, labeled as Daniel Shays and Job Shattuck, leaders of the Massachusetts uprising.
suspect.portrait_src: Daniel Shays and Job Shattuck, woodcut, 1787 · National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution · public domain (CC0)

intro: February 1787. Daniel Shays has vanished into the Massachusetts snow, and the state wants him found.
Twelve years ago he fought for independence. Follow his trail and find out how he became a wanted man.
At every stop, name the principle it shows. At the end, find the one that shows up at the most stops.
Every place, date and document is real.

meter.label: States that have ratified
meter.line: Right principle on the first try: 2 states. After a miss: 1. Nine states ratify the Constitution.

stops.story: Shays is a Massachusetts teenager when Britain wins its war with France and is left with the bill.

clue.text: Open the Atlas: The Proclamation Line of 1763.

ask.prompt: What does the gray-blue color on the map stand for?
options: Land the Crown reserved for Native nations
Land the colonies could sell to settlers
hints: Find the key on the map.
Who was the land set aside for?

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Britain, deep in war debt, taxed the colonies to pay for defending them (Document 2), but colonists elected no one to Parliament: Representative Government.

stops.evidence: 1765 · Britain taxes the colonies to pay for defending them · Document 2 · Representative Government

stops.story: In 1775 Shays's militia company marches to Boston. That June he fights at Bunker Hill.

ask.prompt: How is Boston joined to the mainland?
options: By a thin strip of land called Boston Neck
By a long bridge to Cambridge
hints: Look for the narrowest strip of land on the map.
It's named after a part of the body.

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Revere sold a one-sided picture of the 1770 shooting (Document 4). Freedom of the press protects it: Individual Rights.

stops.evidence: 1770 · Revere sells a one-sided picture of the shooting · Document 4 · Individual Rights (civil liberties)

stops.story: Captain Shays fights at Saratoga in 1777, but the army can't pay him in full. He leaves in 1780.

ask.prompt: What is the July 1776 stop called?
hints: Look at the stops dated 1776.
Read the line from “Remember the ladies” to the next stop.

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Document 8 says people have “certain rights that cannot be taken away.” Rights you're born with are Natural Rights.

stops.evidence: 1776 · Rights no government can take away · Document 8 · Natural Rights

stops.story: Why wasn't Shays paid? The country's first plan of government gave Congress no power to tax.

ask.prompt: Which article says how the national government gets its money?
hints: Look for the word “taxes.”
It's the article about the costs of war.

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Articles II and VIII leave the states their power and their taxes (Document 11). Splitting power between nation and states is Federalism.

stops.evidence: 1781 · The states keep the power to tax · Document 11 · Federalism

stops.story: Massachusetts taxes farmers hard, and courts take farms for debt. In 1786 armed farmers close the courts. In January 1787 Shays and about 1,500 men march on the Springfield arsenal and are driven off.

clue.text: Open the Threads map. Follow the line from the Articles to the Constitution.

ask.prompt: What kind of connection is that line?
hints: Look at the tag on the line.
Did one help bring about the other?

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: When armed men shut the courts, the law stops working for everyone — and Washington asks what protects a man's life, liberty or property then (Document 12). That is Rule of Law.

stops.evidence: 1786–1787 · Farmers close the courts · Document 12 · Rule of Law
stops.nearMiss: You just missed him. Shays has escaped north, to Vermont.

stops.story: While Shays hides in Vermont, delegates meet in Philadelphia to write a new plan of government.

ask.prompt: Which section gives Congress the power to “lay and collect taxes”?
hints: “Lay” a tax means set a tax. Look for the word “taxes.”
It's the last section in the document.

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Section 8 lets Congress “lay and collect taxes” (Document 14). Now Congress can tax too, not just the states: Federalism.

stops.evidence: 1787 · Now Congress can tax too, not just the states · Document 14 · Federalism

door.text: The Constitution needs nine states to ratify. Both sides argue in the newspapers.

question.stem: Hamilton (Document 13) and an Antifederalist (Document 16) disagree. What are they arguing about?
options: How much power the national government should have
Whether to declare independence from Britain
Whether to end the slave trade
hints: Hamilton says the states' failures stopped “all the wheels of the national government.”
The Antifederalist fears “unbounded” power.
question.why: Too weak, or too strong? That fight decides the vote.

ratified: June 21, 1788: New Hampshire is the ninth state. The Constitution is ratified.
And Shays? He's pardoned that same year.
door.short: Ratified anyway: in June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state. Your pair was {n} states short of nine. History didn't wait, but your case for it was weaker.
door.short_one: Ratified anyway: in June 1788, New Hampshire became the ninth state. Your pair was 1 state short of nine. History didn't wait, but your case for it was weaker.

acts.title: Act II · The new government's first tests, 1788–1825
intro: Pardoned in 1788, Shays later moves to western New York.
The new government can tax now. How far does its power reach?
Two more stops. No meter: just the trail.

stops.story: In 1798, fearing war with France, the party in power makes some criticism of the government a crime.

clue.text: Open the Threads map. Follow the line from the Bill of Rights to the Sedition Act.

ask.prompt: The line says the Sedition Act tests five words. Which ones?
hints: Read the line's one-line reason.
They're the first words of the First Amendment.

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: Document 19 makes some criticism of the government a crime. Critics said it broke the promise of free speech and press: Individual Rights.

stops.evidence: 1798 · A law against criticizing the government · Document 19 · Individual Rights (civil liberties)

stops.story: Chief Justice John Marshall's Supreme Court decides how far the national government's power reaches.

ask.prompt: Marshall says the power to tax involves the power to do what?
hints: Find the sentence in quotation marks.
What could a state's tax do to the national bank?

question.stem: Which principle does this stop show?
hints: Not this one. Check each principle's line on the card.
Which line describes what happened here?
question.why: No state may tax or control the national government's lawful work (Document 21). When they clash, valid federal law wins: Federalism.

stops.evidence: 1819 · No state may tax the national government's work · Document 21 · Federalism

final.prompt: Check your tally. Which principle shows up at the most stops? Type its name.
hints: Check your tally. Which principle has the most stops?
Open the Civic Principles card for its name.

after_by_answer.federalism: That's it: Federalism. Federalism: Power is divided between the national government and the states. When they clash, valid federal law wins. Now write your case.

lines: Daniel Shays died in Sparta, New York, in 1825, a poor man.
He lived on a federal pension for his service in the Revolution. A government that can collect taxes can pay its old soldiers.
He's buried in Livingston County, about 50 miles from this room.

reflection: Which principle did you get on the first try, and how?
Rebel or patriot: what would the other side say?
What will you use on the test tomorrow?
